episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Tuesday, April 21, 2026. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Insights and Trends today, artificial intelligence is reshaping how college students choose their academic majors. Forty-two percent of bachelor's degree students have given at least fair thought to changing their major because of A.I.'s impact on the job market, the Lumina Foundation-Gallup 2026 State of Higher Education Study found. Thirteen percent have already made the switch.

The numbers are even higher for associate degree students. Fifty-six percent have reconsidered their field of study, and nearly one in five have already changed majors.

Men are notably more likely than women to report changing majors due to A.I., at twenty-one percent compared to twelve percent. Students in technology programs are most affected, with seventy percent giving at least fair thought to a major change. Those in vocational fields are close behind at seventy-one percent. Students in health care and natural sciences programs were the least likely to report A.I. influencing their major selection decisions.

Meanwhile, A.I. use is now routine on campus even as institutions struggle to set clear policies. Fifty-seven percent of students use A.I. daily or weekly to understand difficult coursework. Sixty percent use it regularly to verify homework answers. Over half use it to edit writing or summarize lectures. Yet forty-two percent of students report their school discourages A.I. use, and eleven percent say it is prohibited outright. Students consistently expect their institutions to prepare them for a workforce where A.I. capabilities are widespread, the survey found.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In A.I. Workforce and Careers, new college graduates are finding jobs faster than last year despite a competitive market. Seventy-seven percent of 2025 graduates landed their job within three months of earning their degree, ZipRecruiter's 2026 grad report found. That's a jump from sixty-three percent the year before.

The improvement comes with caveats. Nearly forty-three percent of college grads ages twenty-two to twenty-seven are underemployed, working jobs that don't require the degree they earned. About one in five say they're overqualified for their current position, and a similar share said they intentionally applied below their level just to get a foothold. The 2025 grads most likely to have found work soon after college majored in agriculture and environmental science, nursing, history or philosophy, and education.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Ethical A.I., Washington University faculty remain divided following the provost office's plus A.I. academic initiative. Vice Dean of Undergraduate Affairs Erin McGlothlin has been developing A.I. principles for Arts and Sciences students and faculty, Student Life reports.

Some professors compare A.I. adoption to previous technological shifts. Assistant Professor Mitra Naseh noted that people adjust and learn how to use new tools, just as they did with search engines. Others express deeper concerns. McGlothlin described A.I. development as feeling like an attack on the writing skills she spent decades cultivating. Teaching Professor Eileen G'Sell expressed concern that students receive mixed messages about appropriate A.I. use across different academic disciplines.

Both McGlothlin and Associate Professor Ila Sheren are plaintiffs in ongoing litigation against Anthropic regarding unauthorized use of their published works for training A.I. models.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Case Study, Agnes Scott College will introduce a three-part A.I. curriculum as part of its required first-year experience beginning this fall. The institution's Universal A.I. initiative emphasizes critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and decision-making rather than training students on specific platforms, Inside Higher Ed reports.

Students will examine issues including bias and fairness, privacy and surveillance, accountability, labor displacement, and environmental impact. Rachel Bowser, vice president of academic affairs and dean of the college, stated that critical thinking and judgment have never been more important and are necessary for discerning use of A.I.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Beyond Ed today, Google is betting forty billion dollars that Anthropic will win the A.I. race. The initial investment of ten billion dollars values Anthropic at three hundred fifty billion dollars, with additional investments tied to milestone achievement, The Motley Fool reported. Google will also provide five gigawatts of its T.P.U. infrastructure.

Anthropic's annual recurring revenue has grown dramatically, from one billion dollars at the end of 2024 to nine billion at the end of 2025, reaching thirty billion dollars as of early April 2026. The company tripled its revenue in just four months. Anthropic reportedly plans a significant public offering later this year.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Thank you for joining us. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.
